newsitem.title: INDIA: ADB sees robust Indian industry growth.
newsitem.headline: ADB sees robust Indian industry growth.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank said on Thursday it expected Indian industry to grow by a robust 11.7 percent in the financial years 1997/98 (April-March) and 1998/99.
"Industry will continue as an engine of economic growth and should increase by 11.5 percent in 1997 and 1998," the ADB said in its annual report on India.
The services sector, which accounts for more than 40 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), is expected to grow by around 6.5 percent during this period, the bank said.
ADB said that since agriculture was an important contributor to GDP growth, monsoons would continue to play an important role.

"Because agriculture remains important, GDP growth continues to be affected by the weather," the bank said, forecasting that GDP growth would be sustained at 7.0 percent in the next two years if the monsoon rains were favourable.
But the bank said inadequate infrastructure was an area of concern.

"Expansion in the power generation industry slowed considerably (in 1996/97), and this may hold back future industrial growth as it did in the past, although manufacturing companies have taken steps to minimise the effects by using diesel generators for their own capital electricity supply."
The bank said private sector must be encourage to take long-term stakes in infrastructure development.

"While domestic resource mobilisation and captial inflows can accelerate economic growth, infrastructure bottlenecks could threaten the sustainibility of such growth," ADB said, adding that there were major constraints in the power, transport and telecommunications sectors.

ADB said the initial vigour of industrial growth, following deregulation and the rationalisation and reduction of import tariffs, had slackened in 1996/97 due to lower export growth, the dampening effect of financial stringency and infrastructure constraints.

"Neverthless the industry sector continued to be the leading sector, although its growth moderated to 8.7 percent in 1996 compared with 11.6 percent in the previous year, the highest rate in 25 years," ADB said.
Growth slowed in 1996/97 as the boom in investment and production of consumer durables goods eased, the bank added.
Delicensing of investments in cars and household durables led to a boom in production, with 37 percent growth in 1995/96.

"In 1996, there were signs that the pent-up demand for consumer durable goods had been substantially met, resulting in more modest growth in domestic production and lower demand for imported capital goods," the bank said.
ADB said tax revenues during 1997/98 were expected to increase by 16.6 percent, despite recently announced cuts in corporate and personal taxes.
"The buoyancy in tax revenues is expected to result from continuing economic growth and a tax base widened by new levies on a range of goods and services."

A projected reduction in the fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP during 1997/98, from 5.0 percent in the previous fiscal year would help lessen the government's need to borrow from the central bank, ADB said.
"This should help contain the rate of money supply growth to 14.5-16.5 percent annually over the next two years."

"In turn, and in the absence of any supply-side shocks, consumer price inflation should remain at around 8.5 percent over this period, and might even move down to 6.5-7.0 percent range as targeted by the government," ADB said.
